clinicalPearls: Recognised by a distinctive bird-like face with a thin, beaked nose, small pinched features, micrognathia and frontal bossing
Congenital cataracts are a cardinal feature, often bilateral, alongside microphthalmia and other ocular abnormalities
Hypotrichosis (sparse hair) including scanty scalp hair, eyebrows and eyelashes, plus skin atrophy, contributes to a progeroid appearance
Dental anomalies are prominent, including natal teeth, hypodontia, malformed teeth and malocclusion
Proportionate short stature is usual and most cases are sporadic, with the molecular basis still incompletely defined
The small mandible and narrow airway create a real risk of upper airway obstruction, especially in infancy and around anaesthesia
Management is supportive and multidisciplinary, focusing on ophthalmic care, airway safety and dental management
reference.pathophysiology: Hallermann-Streiff syndrome is a congenital disorder of craniofacial and ectodermal development whose precise molecular cause is not fully established, with most cases occurring sporadically. Abnormal development of the first branchial arch derivatives and midline craniofacial structures produces the characteristic dyscephaly, beaked nose, micrognathia and dental anomalies, while disturbed ocular development gives congenital cataracts and microphthalmia. Involvement of ectodermal tissues accounts for the sparse hair and atrophic skin that lend the progeroid appearance.
additionalInvestigations: Ophthalmic assessment for congenital cataract, microphthalmia and other ocular anomalies
Craniofacial imaging to characterise the mandible and skull
Airway evaluation, especially before anaesthesia or sedation
Dental assessment for natal teeth and other anomalies
Genetic evaluation to exclude defined progeroid and dysostosis syndromes
redFlags: Upper airway obstruction from micrognathia and a narrow airway, particularly in infancy
Difficult airway during anaesthesia or sedation
Visual deprivation from dense congenital cataracts requiring timely management
Feeding difficulty with faltering growth in early life
reference.prognosis: Intelligence is usually normal and many individuals reach adulthood, but airway problems in infancy, feeding difficulties and visual impairment are important sources of morbidity that require proactive management.
pitfalls: Underestimating the airway risk during anaesthesia because of the small mandible
Delaying cataract management and risking amblyopia in infancy
Confusing the progeroid features with a true progeria and giving inaccurate prognosis
Overlooking natal or malformed teeth that can compromise the airway or feeding
references: Smith's Recognizable Patterns of Human Malformation
management: Proactive airway management given micrognathia and a narrow airway, with careful multidisciplinary anaesthetic planning and treatment of obstructive sleep apnoea
Early ophthalmological assessment with cataract extraction and correction of refractive error to preserve vision
Nutritional support and feeding assistance for infantile feeding difficulties
Dental management of natal teeth and other anomalies with regular paediatric dental care
Growth monitoring and general paediatric surveillance
Coordinated multidisciplinary care across paediatrics, ophthalmology, ENT, anaesthesia and dentistry
Genetic evaluation and counselling to confirm the diagnosis and exclude other progeroid and dysostosis syndromes
